name: Niccolò Machiavelli
summary: Machiavelli served the Florentine Republic as secretary and diplomat and wrote The Prince, a manual of power for rulers, and the Discourses on Livy, which favours a mixed republic with an armed citizenry. He separates political success from conventional morality, defends a citizen militia over mercenaries, and treats religion as a civic tool while criticising the Church's role in Italian division. The Prince and the Discourses differ in sympathy and are read here with the Discourses as closer to his own preference.

sources.author: Niccolò Machiavelli

sources.usedFor: Republicanism, religion, and the neo-Roman reading of liberty.

property-fundamental.rationale: Prince ch. 17 warns rulers never to seize subjects' property, as men forget a father's death sooner than the loss of patrimony; the argument is prudential, so low.

strong-leader.rationale: Contested: Prince advises a decisive ruler and Discourses I.34 praises the dictatorship for acting quickly where ordinary bodies are slow, yet Discourses I.58 prefers a law-bound people to an unbound prince.

state-harmful.rationale: All of Prince and Discourses assume the state is necessary for order and glory; Discourses I.2-I.5 are about building lasting states.

empower-police-military.rationale: He urges a strong, well-armed state under its own citizen troops (Prince chs. 12-14), but Discourses II.10 denies that money is the sinews of war, so funding is not his emphasis.

more-religion-public.rationale: Discourses I.11-15 argue that religion is of great moment to a state and praise the Roman use of it; he blames the Roman Church for Italy's loss of religion. Scholars dispute his personal belief.

gradual-change.rationale: Discourses I.25 says anyone reforming a free state must retain at least the semblance of its old ways; contested by I.9, where one man should found or remake a state alone.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Discourses I.6 and II.3 contrast Rome, which admitted foreigners and grew strong, with Sparta, which closed its borders; I.55 also warns foreign manners corrupt.

nation-first.rationale: Discourses III.41 holds that the country must be defended whether by honour or dishonour, and Prince ch. 18 says to break faith when interest requires.

revolution-justified.rationale: Discourses I.2 recounts rulers overthrown by the nobles and people, and Prince ch. 6 notes that armed innovators succeed; he mostly describes rather than endorses revolution.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Discourses I.55 holds that free government survives where citizens are roughly equal in property, as in Germany and Switzerland; I.37 favours poor citizens, not an explicit programme of small owners.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Discourses I.2 counts principality among the three good forms; Discourses I.58 praises France, whose kings are bound by an infinity of laws; Prince ch. 2 treats hereditary rule as easiest to hold. He nevertheless prefers a republic.

democracy-best.rationale: Contested: Discourses I.2 lists popular government among the six simple forms that are all pernicious, yet I.58 judges a people wiser and more constant than a prince.

political-violence-never.rationale: Discourses I.9 pardons Romulus for killing Remus because done for the common good, and Prince chs. 8 and 17 justify well-used violence and executions.

separate-church-state.rationale: Contested: Discourses I.12 blames the Church's temporal power for dividing Italy, but I.11-15 want rulers to use religion to bind citizens.

military-superiority.rationale: Prince ch. 14: a prince should have no other aim or thought than war and its rules and discipline, since it is the sole art of one who rules.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Discourses I.4 and Prince ch. 9 say every city contains the people and the great with opposed desires, and that this conflict shaped Rome's laws; he does not call it the main driver of history.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Discourses III.41 puts the country's defence before honour or scruple, and I.9 excuses acts done for the common good; no theory of individual rights is stated.

restore-past-order.rationale: Discourses III.1 says states endure only if renewed by returning to their first principles, and the Discourses repeatedly holds up ancient Rome as the model.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Prince ch. 15 chooses the effectual truth of things over imagined ideals and ch. 18 says men judge a ruler by the result.

means-match-ends.rationale: Discourses I.9 defends violent means for a good founding, and Prince ch. 18 judges rulers by outcomes; means need not mirror the aim.

conscription.rationale: Art of War: citizens are enrolled, armed and exercised in arms on holy days; the editor's introduction describes his scheme of drilling all able-bodied men of 17-40. He organised the Florentine militia as secretary.

national-rebirth.rationale: Prince ch. 26 calls for a redeemer to liberate a prostrate Italy, and Discourses III.1 says states survive only when renewed by returning to first principles.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Discourses I.6: a state organised only to maintain itself will fall when forced to expand, and he prefers the Roman model of growth over the Spartan or Venetian; Prince chs. 3 and 14 discuss acquiring territory.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Discourses I.55 calls lords of strongholds with vassals and retainers sworn foes to free institutions; Prince ch. 4 treats feudal barons as a source of danger to a ruler.

bound-labor.rationale: Inferred: Discourses I.55 condemns lords with castles and retainers as enemies of free institutions.

single-common-good.rationale: Discourses I.4 and I.5 argue that the conflict of nobles and people, each with a different humour, produced Rome's liberty, so politics balances competing interests.

rule-by-example.rationale: Prince ch. 12 names good laws and good arms as the foundations of a state, ch. 17 advises inspiring fear, and Discourses III.1 values punishment to renew order; this runs against relying mainly on moral example.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Discourses I.5 says the nobles desire to dominate and the great are a main threat to liberty, and I.55 condemns idle gentlemen; no claim that elites are out of touch.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Inferred: He assigns the state expansion, civic religion and the shaping of citizens' character (Discourses I.6, I.11-15), well beyond defence and justice.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Prince ch. 18 holds that a ruler must use force as well as law, and Discourses I.9 excuses violent founding acts; he never treats initiating force as wrong.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Discourses I.4 credits conflict between nobles and commons with Rome's freedom, and I.6 argues that a republic free from war would grow effeminate and divided.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Inferred: Discourses I.5 says the people desire not to be dominated and prefer liberty, and scholars (SEP) link him to freedom as non-domination, but he does not define it.

separated-powers.rationale: Discourses I.2 and I.34 describe Rome's consuls, senate and tribunes as bodies that checked one another, and he treats this balance as the reason for its stability.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Discourses I.34 praises the Roman dictatorship, which gave one man power in danger to decide without advice and act without appeal, as a safeguard that helped the republic.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Inferred: Discourses I.6 praises Rome for admitting foreigners and increasing its citizens, preferring this to Sparta's exclusion.

people-in-arms.rationale: Prince chs. 12-13, Discourses I.21 (a reproach to lack a national army) and the Art of War urge replacing mercenaries with armed citizens; he organised the Florentine militia.

death-penalty.rationale: Prince ch. 17 allows taking life with proper justification and manifest cause, and Discourses III.1 values exemplary punishment to restore a republic to its principles.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Discourses I.12 says the Church kept Italy divided and corrupt, and I.11-15 praise Roman rulers who used religion for the state; he does not propose specific measures.

character-from-environment.rationale: Discourses III.46 says the persistence of a family's character cannot be ascribed wholly to blood but to the different training and education children receive.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Contested: Discourses I.58 holds that rulers bound by laws (as in France) are better than unbound ones, while Prince ch. 18 advises breaking faith when advantageous. The Discourses is taken as closer to his own view.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Discourses I.2: calls all six simple forms of government pernicious and praises legislators who chose a form combining monarchic, aristocratic and popular elements, as in Rome.

land-redistribution.rationale: Discourses I.37 blames the Agrarian Law, with its retroactive seizure of estates, for ruining Rome, though it also says it restrained the nobles' ambition; contested.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Discourses I.12 laments that Italy could never be brought under one head and Prince ch. 26 urges liberating Italy; applies to Italians, not peoples in general.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Discourses I.55: a commonwealth cannot be founded where idle landed gentlemen with castles and retainers exist unless they are first got rid of; but Prince shows rulers relying on nobles, so contested.

elective-rulers.rationale: Discourses I.10 observes that emperors who succeeded by birth were bad (except Titus) and those chosen by adoption were good, favouring selection by merit; Prince ch. 2 still accepts hereditary rule, so the evidence is mixed.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Prince ch. 9 says a prince should keep the people friendly, since they ask only not to be oppressed, and ch. 19 stresses avoiding hatred; he also stresses force and fraud.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Discourses I.55 and III.25 praise frugal civic life and blame luxury and foreign manners for corruption; no direct argument about consumer goods.

non-intervention.rationale: Prince ch. 3 advises a ruler to make himself head and defender of weaker neighbours and weaken the stronger, i.e. to intervene in neighbours' affairs for advantage.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Contested: Prince ch. 8 and ch. 17 justify eliminating rivals, while Discourses I.4 praises the popular tumults and I.7 values open accusations.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Discourses I.14 praises the Romans for punishing those who rashly slighted religion; he treats this as civic policy rather than doctrine.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Prince ch. 14 and Art of War treat armed strength as the foundation of any state; Prince ch. 12 says good arms are essential.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Prince ch. 21: it is more advantageous to declare for one of two powerful neighbours than to stand neutral.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Discourses I.10 says the five good emperors came by adoption and ruin returned when the empire passed to heirs by birth; contested by Prince ch. 2, which finds hereditary states easiest to keep.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Discourses I.58 praises the French kingdom for its security under an infinity of laws binding the king; the Roman dictatorship (I.34) is an emergency exception, so mixed.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Discourses I.37 says a well-governed commonwealth keeps the state rich and citizens poor, and I.55 says wealthy gentlemen with castles are sworn foes of free government.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Discourses I.12 says it is of much moment to make account of religion and that its loss ruined Italy; he would not have the state undermine it.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Art of War has young men exercised in arms on holy days to serve in a citizen army, but it does not describe uniformed youth movements.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Inferred: Discourses III.41 holds that the country must be defended by any means, and Art of War trains citizens to fight; he does not address individual self-defence.

second-chamber.rationale: Discourses I.2 and I.5 praise the Roman mix of consuls, senate and people; he does not specify modern two-chamber design.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Contested: Art of War advises making war to have peace and not seeking war, but Discourses I.6 and Prince ch. 3 endorse expansion and anticipating enemies.

arms-reduction.rationale: Prince ch. 14 and Discourses I.21 stress being strongly armed, and Art of War seeks a trained citizen army; he does not recommend low armaments.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Inferred: Prince ch. 18 advises breaking faith when interest requires and Discourses III.42 says promises made under compulsion need not be kept.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Inferred: Art of War demands strict discipline, with death for soldiers who break ranks in fear, so he would not allow refusal of orders.

simple-living.rationale: Discourses I.55 praises regions content with the produce of their own land and uncorrupted by foreign manners, and III.25 praises the poverty of Cincinnatus.

notes: The Prince (advice to a prince) and the Discourses (republicanism) differ on the people, law-bound rule and succession; scholarly consensus treats the Discourses as closer to his own preference, and contested items are low or 0. Inferred answers are marked in the rationale. His personal religious belief is disputed.
